summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for monitoring MIB objects and taking action through events.

plainLanguage.summary: This lets a device watch its own numbers and react when something goes wrong.

questions: how to trigger events from mib objects
how does the event mib trigger work
what is the difference between existence boolean and threshold triggers
subtitle: A table-driven way for a device to watch its own MIB values and fire notifications or set other values when a condition is met.

tldr.problem: Network managers need devices to watch MIB objects, on themselves or on other systems, and react when something changes, without a manager polling constantly.
tldr.mechanism: The Event MIB defines tables of triggers (existence, boolean and threshold tests), groups of objects to attach, and events that send an SNMP notification, set a MIB object, or both.
tldr.outcome: It extends the RMON alarm and event groups with remote targets, wildcards, booleans and set actions. It is a Proposed Standard and the text records no replacement.

today: RFC 2981 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion for building the values to monitor is RFC 2982.

sections.title: What the Event MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 2981 defines a MIB module, DISMAN-EVENT-MIB, for use with SNMP. It gives a system the ability to monitor MIB objects on the local system or on a remote system and take simple action when a trigger condition is met.

The RFC argues that networks have grown well beyond what people can manage directly, so automated, distributed management is vital. A system watching itself, or being watched by another system, is an important part of that. The design suits either a relatively powerful manager or mid-level manager, and also a somewhat more limited self-managing system.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a person staring at a screen all day, the machine keeps an eye on its own numbers and speaks up when something needs attention.

sections.title: Relationship to RMON and Other MIBs
sections.content:
The Event MIB is based on experience with the RMON MIB (RFC 1757) and provides a superset of the RMON alarm and event groups. What RMON called alarms, the Event MIB calls triggers. Triggers keep RMON's handling of thresholds and add booleans. Events keep RMON's idea of sending an SNMP notification and add the idea of setting a MIB object. The key extension is that alarms can be generated for objects on another network element.

It is also the successor and update to the Manager-to-Manager MIB (RFC 1451), which the text says was declared Historic pending this work. It depends on the SNMPv3 Management Target and Notification MIBs (RFC 2573).

The companion RFC 2982 (Expression MIB) is the expected source of boolean objects to monitor. The two overlap in wildcard and delta sample capabilities, so a careful implementation might share code for them.
sections.plainLanguage: It is the grown-up version of an older alarm system. It keeps what worked and adds the ability to watch other machines and to do something about a problem, not just report it.

sections.title: Triggers, Objects and Events
sections.content:
The MIB has four sections: triggers, objects, events and notifications. Triggers define the conditions that lead to events, and events may cause notifications.

  • The trigger table lists what objects are monitored and how, and relates each trigger to an event. Companion tables hold extra settings that depend on the test type (delta, existence, boolean, threshold).
  • The objects table lists objects that can be added to notifications, selected by trigger, by trigger test, or by event.
  • The event table defines what happens when an event fires: send a notification, set a MIB object, or both.
  • The notification section defines generic notifications and the objects carried in them.

Entries are indexed by an owner string (mteOwner) plus a name. Triggers and events are referenced by owner and name, and an empty name means no event or no extra objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of three lists. One says what to watch, one says what extra facts to include in a message, and one says what to do when the watch goes off.

sections.title: How Triggers Are Tested
sections.content:
Each trigger names an object to sample (mteTriggerValueID) and how often (mteTriggerFrequency, in seconds, default 600). The sample is either an absoluteValue or a deltaValue, the difference between two samples. The RFC says SNMP counters should be sampled as deltas to be meaningful. A trigger is created disabled by default and does nothing until mteTriggerEnabled is true.

Three tests can be selected in mteTriggerTest:

  • existence fires when the object appears, vanishes or changes value. It will not fire again for appearance or absence until the object has been in the other state.
  • boolean compares the value to a configured value using unequal, equal, less, lessOrEqual, greater or greaterOrEqual. It fires when the result is true and does not fire again until the result has gone false and come back to true.
  • threshold uses rising and falling thresholds, plus separate delta rising and falling thresholds. After a rising event, another is not triggered until the value falls below the threshold and reaches the falling threshold, and the reverse for falling.

A startup control for each test decides whether a condition that is already true when the entry becomes active may fire an event.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask three kinds of questions: did the thing show up or disappear, is the number bigger or smaller than my line, or did it cross a high line or a low line. The alarm only rings again after the number has gone back across the other line.

sections.title: Remote Targets and Wildcards
sections.content:
Monitoring can be local or remote. Remote monitoring uses the tag service of the Management Target MIB to select systems and works like an ordinary SNMP management application. A target tag of length 0 means the local system. A system that only manages itself MAY not implement remote monitoring.

A wildcard is an object identifier with part or all of its instance portion left off. The system should then use a GetNext-type operation to find the zero or more instances it matches, as an ordinary SNMP application would. Each instance is treated as if it were a separate entry. For example, a wildcarded object can trigger an event that sets another wildcarded object, and the instance that fired the trigger is the one used for the set. Context names can be wildcarded by leaving characters off the end, which the RFC notes may not be supported for remote systems.

The compliance statement lets implementations make the target-tag and wildcard objects read-only, so a system may skip wildcarding or limit monitoring to the local system or pre-configured remote systems.
sections.plainLanguage: A wildcard is like saying watch every light switch in the house instead of naming each one. The machine finds all of them itself and treats each as its own alarm.

sections.title: Events, Notifications and Errors
sections.content:
An event entry has an actions setting (mteEventActions) with two bits: notification and set. For notification, Traps and/or Informs are sent according to the SNMP Notification MIB. For set, an SNMP Set is performed on a configured object, with a configured integer value, locally or at a target.

The MIB defines five notifications: mteTriggerFired (boolean or existence triggers), mteTriggerRising, mteTriggerFalling, mteTriggerFailure and mteEventSetFailure. Each carries the trigger name, target name, context name, object identifier and either the value or a failure reason.

The two failure notifications are for diagnosis only. The text says a manager must enable them only with a certain fear and trembling, because they can easily crowd out more important information. They are meant to help find problems indicated by the error counters.

Counters such as mteTriggerFailures and mteEventFailures track failed attempts, and resource objects let an administrator limit the minimum sampling interval and the number of sampled instances.
sections.plainLanguage: When the alarm goes off the machine can send a message to the boss, flip a switch, or both. It also keeps a tally of times it tried and failed, but you should only turn on the failure messages when you are hunting for a problem.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Security of Event MIB entries depends on SNMPv3 access control, either for the whole MIB or for subsets chosen by entry owner name. The owner string can be mapped to a securityName or groupName in the View-Based Access Control Model (RFC 2575).

Access to monitored objects depends on the Management Target MIB for remote systems. For local objects without a target tag, the system uses the security credentials recorded from whoever made the entry active, and MUST conceptually use isAccessAllowed to make sure it does not violate security. The formal Security Considerations section only points back to the Security section and the object descriptions.
sections.plainLanguage: The alarm can only look at things its creator was allowed to look at, so setting one up does not give anyone a secret way to peek at private numbers.

items.label: unequal
items.desc: True when the sampled value differs from the configured value (the default).

items.label: equal
items.desc: True when the sampled value equals the configured value.

items.label: less
items.desc: True when the sampled value is less than the configured value.

items.label: lessOrEqual
items.desc: True when less than or equal.

items.label: greaterOrEqual
items.desc: True when greater than or equal.
